speechtext:
I think my hon. friend
(Mr. Oliver) is in error. The figures of enlistment given are of men who have enlisted, passed the medical examination, and been enrolled. I think the hon. gentleman is wrong-I say it with all respect for him -in the effect he gives to the term "wastage." That term refers to men who have gone to the front and have afterwards been incapacitated for service, and their places taken by those held in reserve. It refers to men who were fit for service and have been rendered unfit, and not merely those who were physically unfit at the time they were enlisted. The man who passes the medical examination and is accepted must be assumed to be fit; he has been accepted as a fighting man.

My argument does not
rest on the question whether rejections were many or few. I am willing to accept the figures that are given. But I must

take some figures. I quite agree with the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that the figures given by the Prime Minister show the number of men who passed the medical examination and were enrolled. But of these men some have been found to be unfit before they reached the firing line. My judgment would be that we are not entitled to count these men as our contribution toward the winning of the war. No matter how good the intentions of these men may have been, they have not helped to win the war, on the contrary, they have been, in proportion to their numbers, an enormous charge upon the treasury and to that extent have prevented the winning of the war. But it is not for me to argue that point; my point is that the Government's promise-or I would rather say the country's promise-of 500,000 men has not yet been implemented and the Government has not come forward with any proposal looking either directly or indirectly to the fulfilling of that promise. Whether the number needed be many or few, that fact remains without argument, and I still maintain that the men who have not been qualified to go into the fighting line slhould mot, in honesty and fairness1, be counted by us as a contribution to the fighting forces of the Allies. Moreover, they have been a burden upon our resources instead of being a 'Strength to our Allies.
It may be said that this inaction of the Government in regard to the fulfilment of our promise is not a serious matter. It is true that National Service cards have been sent out. There lhas been a great deal of discussion about them; some of them have been answered and some have not. It has been said that, in any oase, no harm1 has been done. Unfortunately, that is not the fact; the discussion that lhas arisen and that has circulated, so to speak, around this National Service proposal has done a great deal of harm- Instead of the National Service proposal being a .measure in aid even of industrial conscription, if you like, or compulsory industrial service, the effect of it has been to decrease in large measure the industrial power of the country Our friends, if I may be permitted to make this suggestion-I cannot come to any other conclusion-talking of compulsion in one part of dhe country and talking no compulsion in the other part, have unfortunately convinced the people in one part of the country that compulsion is impending, with the result that those who do not desire to submit to compulsion, either

industrial or military, have, by simply exercising tlheir powers of locomotion and stepping across the line, put themselves out of the reach of compulsion either industrial or military. I will not dwell on this subject at any great length, but it has reached such a point that the Government itself saw fit to publish in tihe newspapers of Canada on the opening day of Parliament a declaration to reassure the people that National Service did not mean compulsory service either for industrial or military purposes. The idea that was first given out that National Service meant fulfilling our promise of 500,000 fighting men gradually dwindled, until now it does not mean any kind of service at all; and the Prime Minister when 'he discusses the reply to the Address does not even allude to win at at one time was considered to be a most important and vital question, and one that, to quote the ex-Minister of Militia, might fairly be considered to be bis baby.
The question may reasonably be asked: we have not fulfilled our promise; what is proposed to be done about it? I am not charged with the responsibility of directing the affairs of this country, or with the responsibility of having originated this National Service proposal, which has done no good, has done so much harm, and has finally died in the hands of those who brought it forth. But I will say this: when the war begun we undertook to play our part in that war by voluntary service. My contention is that under voluntary service we have done wonders, and the greatest wonder of all is that we have done so much under the adverse conditions. Voluntary service has never had a chance, in this country under the administration of our friends. For my own part I have said in this House before, and I am prepared to say it again, that in the case of such a world struggle as we are now engaged in National Service is the only logical service; National Service, I say, that will call up the manhood of the nation for military service. But it must be recognized that there are many things that are right in theory that it is not possible to put into practice. I do not challenge the Government because they have not put conscription in force, although they talked it, hinted at it, and tried to get credit for it without doing it. The fault I have to find is that, depending on voluntary service, we never gave voluntary service a fair chance. It would take too long to cover the different features of the system of enlistment that has prevailed to show in how many ways the

enthusiasm of our people has been slapped in the face by the method of administration of our military affairs. We have heard to-day something of the position in which our forces find themselves in England or in France. Nothing has been said in regard to what has occurred in England or in France that compares in any degree with what has occurred right here in Canada under our own administration of our own military affairs amongst our own people. If there is any other way in which enlistment could be discouraged at the hands of our military administration, I have not yet heard of it and I am unable to conceive of it. Such enlistment as has taken place- speaking of experience within my own knowledge-has taken place because of the sense of duty that has arisen in the minds of the men who have given themselves for the service. Men have travelled hundreds of miles on foot in the country in which I live to offer themselves as soldiers of the Empire.
They have come into the city of Edmonton-this was in the early days of the war- responding to the call which was sent out, expecting that their services were needed. They have come in without money; they have been told that they were not needed; they have been unable to .secure employment, and have had to accept charity, these men who had offered their lives to serve the country. Times changed, and where in those days men travelled hundreds of miles and offered themselves and were refused- and I may say were refused with insult in many cases-last winter there were established in the city of Edmonton recruiting headquarters for, I think, six separate battalions-this number of battalions to be recruited all at once in a small place. What was the result? Competition amongst the officers to secure the filling up of their contingents; men who were not physically fit were, in many cases, taken on for the purpose of filling up the ranks. Instead of the service being kept at a high level, it was allowed to deteriorate, and the difficulty of filling the regiments became greater as time went on. Not only so, but while these battalions were recruiting in Edmonton, other units from all over the Dominion of Canada were authorized to go in there and set up recruiting offices and call for men. At the present time there is a battalion recruiting in Edmonton, with headquarters some place in New Brunswick-the Macleans, I think it is. Then recently I saw that the Camerons had a recruiting office in Edmonton. While officers were authorized to recruit these six
battalions in Edmonton, their efforts were made more difficult by every conceivable branch of the service being authorized to establish recruiting offices in that city. On top of that there comes the policy that these battalions, which have been gathered under the direction and control of certain officers, are to be broken up, that the recruiting of *a battalion is only a matter of form; that the recruiting of the battalions is only in name, that it is only the gathering up of so many men, and when they are gathered up and taken across they cease to have any identity or any relation to the locality from which they come. Why such a policy was ever introduced it is impossible to say, but surely it would strike anyone 9 p.m. that the idea of locality and of personal associations would be the strongest element in securing the enlistment of men who were going out to risk their lives, and whose lives would depend in large measure upon the faithfulness of the comrades who were with them-surely above everything else an effective recruiting policy would consider the idea of gathering men together from the same locality, men of mutual relationship, men who would have confidence and faith in each other under extreme circumstance.,. Under such circumstances, if they were serving under trusted officers we might expect to get the benefit of the idea of locality and the idea of family relationship-of every idea that produces enthusiasm and willingness to serve. Everybody knows, it is historic, that over one hundred years ago the British Government raised regiments in the highlands of Scotland, at that time none too loyal to the then reigning house. Absolutely on that idea and with that ideal, regiments were raised whose names and whose fame have come down through more than one hundred years, until to-day they are names to conjure with. Surely what was good policy in those days is good policy down to this very day, because we read in the accounts of the fighting that is going on descriptions of the work of this regiment and that regiment and the other regiment, the work of the Sussex, of the Middlesex, of the Suffolks, of the Norfolks, men whose name means something to the localities from which they came. Surely the principle that is so sound and good in the British Islands might .have been found of some use in Canada. But it was not. It was not only ignored, but it seemed that the authorities absolutely went out of their way to discredit it in every form, shape and manner.

Just one word with regard to the-position of the officers who have been authorized to raise battalions. It may be that some may have been authorized as officers to raise battalions who did not have military experience and whose appointment was not warranted by the circumstances. I shall say nothing of that. I assume that the man who was appointed to raise a battalion was the right man to appoint for the purpose, and the fact that he did raise the battalion is evidence that in that respect at any rate he was the right man for the purpose. I have in mind a man who has served for many years, first in the British Army, and afterwards in the Northwest Mounted Police and then in the South African war. Finally he was authorized to raise a battalion at Edmonton, On the strength of his military experience and on the strength of his personal standing, he did raise a battalion without any serious difficulty. Surely such a man with such a battalion, raised under such circumstances-surely it would be right and proper that that battalion should go to the front intact under such leadership.
Does the hon. gentleman not know why battalions were broken up?
I do not know why that one was.

I can give a little information. When word would come in from the front that ten thousand or fifteen thousand or twenty thousand men were needed as reinforcements, the brigade officer would come to the battalion officer commanding and say: How many men have you? And he would say, I have two hundred and fifty. How many have you? I have two hundred and fifty. How many have you? I have five hundred. He takes the men. What would you do? Would you . say because the whole battalion could not go that nobody could go at all, and that the men at the front should not be reinforced?

I am not a military man like my hon. friend, and I cannot give him an answer in that respect. But I think if his suggestion is well founded and that out of a whole battalion in training in England only two hundred and fifty men would be available, it is rather an unfortunate situation.

Some men had joined perhaps six months before and some three. The men who had been drilling for six months might be fit, but the other might
 -
not have had training in bayonet drill or bombing. What would you do with them? Would you send them into the trenches and murder them?

I am afraid that my hon. friend and I cannot come to an understanding on this point. I do not know whether he ever heard of the definition of metaphysics. Metaphysics was defined' by one Scotchman to another in this way: when you hear two men arguing together, if the one that is listening does not know what the other is talking about, and if the other does not know either, that is metaphysics. My hon. friend will forgive me if we do not pursue this discussion- I was not arguing at the moment at all on the merits of the policy; I was arguing as to the consequences to the officers who were placed in that position, who, having been authorized to raise a battalion, having raised that battalion, having taken it to England expecting to render service in the capacity in which they were authorized by this Government, find themselves with the battalion taken away from them, find themselves in Great Britain without occupation, find themselves there, discredited, with or without reason. I ask this House what is the position of other officers recruiting other regiments when this is recognized as their probable fate. I have in mind men who gave up good business in Edmonton in order to, as they believed, serve their country; who were authorized to raise battalions, did raise them, went to England, had their battalions taken away from them. These men had some ambition, I suppose, to serve their country, had some ambition possibly to do credit to their families, their relatives and their friends, but as long as they live, as long as their children live after them, they will never get over the disgrace that has been placed upon them by the action of this Government. How can they say whether the battalion was taken from them because of their inefficiency or because of other reasons? There is no way that these men can justify themselves to the people from amongst whom they come. A more unmerciful, a more outrageous, exercise of authority never was perpetrated.
How could there be success in recruiting if the men upon whom the country depended for success were dealt with in the manner in which they have been dealt with by the Administration of my hon. friend?
You wonder that there has not been more recruiting? It is a miracle that there has been as much recruiting as there

has. Sentiment has a great deal to do with enlistment. Enthusiasm must be aroused or men will not make the sacrifice. It has been the policy in the conduct of this war to in every way prevent the arousing of enthusiasm. I do not speak of the action of this Government; I speak of the action of the Government across the seas, coincided in by our friends here. I speak of the censorship. If there is one thing that people are entitled to know, it is the truth. If there is one thing that people are entitled to know in regard to military operations, in regard to military sacrifices, it is the truth; and it has been the policy, since the opening of this war, on that side of tlhe Atlantic and on this side, to use the power of government to not only conceal the truth, to not only prevent the truth from being expressed, but, worse than that; instead of the censorship being used for its legitimate purpose of preventing military information from reaching the enemy, the censorship has been used for the purpose of protecting those in authority from the consequence of their incompetence and inefficiency at the hands of an informed and outraged public. I do not hold our friends here responsible for that except that they are co-partners in an iniquity that has done more harm to the military enthusiasm of this Dominion than all other causes put together.
It is a serious matter to speak of these questions, but we are in serious circumstances and if we are to meet the conditions that still face us, we must learn from what has taken place in the past and those of us who stand on the floor of Parliament will be doing less than our duty if we do not declare in what way there have been shortcomings on our part or on the part of those who are even higher up than we are. It is our right to know the truth and not have the authority of the Government of Canada or of the Empire used to suppress the truth or to distort the truth or try to conceal the iniquitous incompetence of those in authority.
I will not weary the House by going into further reasons why voluntary enlistment has not succeeded to the extent that it was hoped it would. Enough has been said to prove that the voluntary system has not had a fair trial in this country and that if we are to implement our promise of 50j,000 men we must change our methods in regard to voluntary enlistment, bring ourselves more into line with the sentiment of the people, deal honestly and fairly by the people, give
everybody concerned a square deal and then we may expect, if we can ever expect, to meet the conditions that we have to face.
I said a little while ago that I did not wish to be considered as criticising the Government, simply as the Government. I speak of the Government as tlh.e directors of the affairs of the people. I consider the .people of Canada as partners with -the Government in so far as tlhe administration of war affairs has gone and in so far as the Government has not been criticised for the administration of those affairs. The time has come, it seems to me, when we must criticise if we are going to improve. We must talk plainly and frankly; and the Government, being the Government, must of course take the brunt of criticism. But I do not wish to absolve the people of Canada at large, nor ourselves on this side of the House in so far as we may be responsible for conditions as they are.
The question arises, what is best to be done to bring about an improvement, and first of all, what is the reason that things are as they are? As I said, I hold the Government responsible only as I hold the people responsible. The Government has failed in many respects because the people have not been awake to the exigencies and urgencies of the case. Had the people of Canada been more alive to the conditions as they exist, hai they criticised the Government more freely in time of war, there is no doubt that we should have had more efficient and more energetic action at the hands of the Government. The Government of to-day is the mind of the Parliament of to-day, and the Parliament of today is the mind of the people as it, was over five years ago. We have a parliament elected under peace conditions, when there was no thought of war; we have in power a Government representing the mind of that Parliament, and carrying on the affairs of this country and administering its share of the war in the year 1917 on the ideas of 1911. It is not reasonable to expect that this Parliament elected as it was at that time, and this Government, representing the mind of Parliament as it was at that time, could by any possibility have the point of view of the people of this country at the present time. We have a peace Administration in office, when above everything else we ought to have a war Administration in office. We should have a Parliament elected by the people who have learned, in this last year above all others,

what war means, who know the sacrifices that war calls for, and who know that those sacrifices are the only means whereby wars can be won. If we are to have an effective war administration of our affairs we must go back to the people and get their mandate as their mind is to-day. What has occurred in Great Britain has occurred in Canada. The Parliament of Great Britain, as it was, was elected under conditions of peace, and the Government of Great Britain, as it was, came to power under conditions of peace. When war broke out, that Government and that Parliament dealt with the war conditions from a peace standpoint. It is not possible to win wars by peace methods. Wars must be won by war, and the people of Great Britain have had occasion twice since the war began to take such measures as to bring those in authority more in line with the idea of winning the war by war; until in Great Britain .today, in free Britain, Britain which has laid the foundation of the world's liberty and given the example of constitutional government to the world, to-day in Great Britain, under the stress of war, we have, with the consent of the people, a dictatorship as absolute as it was in the days of Cromwell, for the purpose of winning the war, and as the only means of winning the war.
They have not appealed to the people in Great Britain. It is not for me to say whether they should or should not. But I say this: that in Canada we do not want a dictatorship. We want to continue as a free democracy, and in order to do that we must rest our Parliament upon the mandate of the people; we must bring our Parliament and our Government in line with the mind of the people of to-day. With 70,000 casualties, spread over Canada from ocean to ocean, which is a pretty thick sprinkling in the homes of our country, and with nearly
20,000	of the pick of our manhood having passed out of our lives* there is no doubt that the people of oanaua to-day are not the people they were a year ago. They do not look at the war to-day as they did a year ago; they have different ideas, and it is right that they should have an expression of those ideas through a new Parliament. We do not want a dictatorship in this country, no matter how great the man may be. We want free government, and the only free government is government by the people; government by the people as expressed at the polls. I am at a loss to know for what reason the people of Canada are not con-

sidered to be the best judges of the welfare of Canada. Canada is made up of its people. It is the people of Canada who are paying for the war in money and in blood. There is no authority higher than the people to whom we can go for guidance or direction in this case. It is only reasonable, then, that, when we have come to a point where we have found ourselves unable to fulfil the promise solemnly made by us to ourselves and to our Allies as to the part that we should take in this war, we should go to the people and get their mandate as to winning the war.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (North Cape Breton) :
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I feel a little hoarse to-night, if it would be agreeable to the leader of the Government, I would like to move the adjournment of the debate, although, of course it is my duty to go on.

I am sure I would be very pleased to oblige my hon. friend, but it is very early, and as we adjourned last night at a very early hour, we would like to get on. If my hon. friend would go on for a while, we would consider adjournment later on.

Mr. Speaker, I regret that I have to address you for the first time under more or less physical disability on account of a cold, and I also regret that the leader of the House does not think it advisable to consider the physical condition in which I find myself. I will, however, deal briefly with the question which is before the House; but before entering upon any discussion of the subject more particularly before us, let me follow the precedent of the right hon. leader of the Government and the right hon. leader of the Opposition in congratulating yourself, Sir, upon the high office to which you have been elevated as the first Commoner of this great country of ours. Let me hope, Sir, in following in the path of the great and learned men who have occupied the position which you now occupy, that for the sake of our beloved province by the sea, the precedents which you establish shall do honour and justice to that fair province of which you and I and all other Nova Scotians are so justly proud. The province of Nova Scotia has given great men to the service of this nation. She has given three premiers to the Dominion of Canada and she has given great, capable, and efficient men to the heads of the various important departments of the administration of this country. But, Sir, this is the first time within my memory

that the province of Nova Scotia has furnished a Speaker to this House.
It has been my good fortune to Jive under three sovereigns, eight prime ministers of the Dominion of Canada, and to have occupied a iseai in this House under five Speakers. My experience is that Speakers are more autocratic in their ways and manners than even sovereigns or prime ministers. That is no doubt attributable to the fact that they have a more lively and clear appreciation of tlheir own importance and responsibilities. I am sure, Sir, from the knowledge that I have of you as a young man of education and ability, that - you will, although not I hope in an autocratic .manner or in any domineering way, carry forward in your career .as a Speaker of this House the traditions of those who have gone before. I am glad even at this late hour-il will not call it the eleventh hour of the life of this Government; I think it is nearer the twelfth hour of the life o.f this 'Government-that they are beginning to realize that we have some men of prom. inenee in the province of Nova Scotia. So far the right .hon. leader of the Government has not been willing to give us any great recognition; buit now, even at this late hour, I am pleased that he is beginning to recognize that we have such men. It is not the long bow of the leader of the Government to have a high appreciation .of the men we have in Nova Scotia, and indeed it is rather his weakness that he has not a proper .appreciation of the men that we have in Canada, for it is not iso very long ago since he put himself on record as telling us that there'were a few things we could do in a quiet, domestic way, but that when it came to breaking out into new industries, such as the building of ships, and the preparing of warships and getting ourselves into a proper state of defence, it would' be at least fifty years, when the present generation and the present Parliament would alii be dead, before we could begin. That was rather discouraging news lor the people of Nova Scotia, who have mot been accustomed to that sort of thing. In Nova -Scotia, we have been .accustomed to very much like the idea of the Irishman who was put into competition as to how well he could take a man's measure. The Englishman had one way and the Scotchman had .another, and then the Irishman said: " Why, isir, if you could show me the corner around which a man went I could take his .measure and make him a suit of clothes." It has been
E
cur habit in Nova Scotia to adapt ourselves quickly to circumstances and get along with any new enterprise, and it would be almost *as easy for you to keep a duck from swimming as to keep a Nova Scotian from building ships and manning them if the opportunity were at all presented.
The speech from the Throne is not very wealthy, nor very fat in materials for the purpose of discussion. There is nothing very new in it and nothing which is of any striking importance to the people of this country. There are, of course, references to the war, which is the all-absorbing topic, not only to the people of this country, but to the people of the whole Empire, and after such eloquent addresses as have been made by the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition, the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), and the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), without mentioning the address of the Prime Minister himself, the question of the war, its requirements an'd our duty in respect to it have been very well threshed out, and there As not the same fresh flavour about discussing it n.ow that there was art the commencement of this discussion, although the debate is not very old,
I come, Sir, from ,a country which has done much for the purpose of enforcing and enabling the people of this country to do themselves proud on the question of the war and the question of the defence of this country. We hear on some occasions that we are participating in this war only as a sort of side-show, and that we are not obliged to put- forth very much effort in a direct way .because the fighting is not so much our-s as it is of the countries on the other side that are directly engaged in it. The Canadian people have not taken that view of the war. We have taken it to be our particular case apd we take it to be the war of oiur country.
In the province of Nova Scotia from which I come, as I say we have done ourselves proud in the number of good men and true whom we have .sent for service of the country. And there is no limit at which we can stop except the final one of the establishment of peace upon the ground upon which we had peace, happiness and security before the war broke, out. That is the only mandate we have from the people of -Nova Scotia in rendering aid either to the Government of the d.ay or to any other Government which may have to deal with the wax. I say we are proud of our soldiers and of what they have done for our country.

We are proud of those .soldiers whether French Canadians, English Canadians, Irish Canadians or Scotch Canadians, who have sprung forward to fight in this common cause for our country -anid- its destiny. We are proud in our perfect confidence that, they will continue to -maintain the traditions of their forefathers and will secure for us a continuation of that freedom which we enjoy.
As to what the duties of the Canadian people are in this regard, I do not think I can set them forth in ;any language of my own that will he half .so appropriate as that used m a message addressed to the Canadian people by my -beloved leader (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) as published in the Canadian Liberal monthly of the current month. I do not propose to read- the whole of that highly-valued message, but will give only that portion of it that bears particularly u-pon the special point I am making, the -duties of the Canadian people in this war:
Canadian fathers, mothers, and wives sacrificed their dear ones, when their dear ones donned the King's uniform; of these, many have given to the cause -the last full measure of devotion and now sleep and will forever sleep in the soil of Old France. The -rest of us owe it to them that we also make sacrifice, sacrifice of feelings, of prejudice, of comfort, of leisure, of gai-ns. Such sacrifice is a better monument to the fallen and wounded than either bronze or marble, and the best monument of all is the s-tern determination that their lives and limbs were not given in vain.
While we claim, and with just cause claim to have done much, our efforts pale almost to nothing when compared with the exertions the almost inconceivable exertions of Great Britain, of France, of Russia and of Italy.
In -those countries there has been a constant effort towards concentration in the one object of bringing the war to a triumphant conclusion. This has produced in France especially not only a growing union of all the forces of the nation, but also a union of souls. Antagonisms which before the war seemed irreconcilable have now well high disappeared, and opinions, even -the most heterogeneous are' now embraced in the sacred union.	*
Let us imitate this noble example. Let us here and now sink passions, prejudices, vain and idle recriminations. Let us when criticism is needed, criticise without bitterness, only by appeals to reason, and- above all le-t us bend all our' energies towards making Canada an effective factor in the struggle.
The heart of the nation must beat with one aocord and one desire. Thus and thus only can Canada attain the full standard of what she owes to herself and her future and with such an inspiration, the people will rise to a consciousness of national power and national character which will be enduring and permanent for the welfare and grandeur of our Dominion.
Whether victory and peace be near or distant, our resolve will not falter. We will continue to the end, calmly, firmly and grimly determined to do our share so that this terrible

scourge of war may forever .pass away from us. And there is - hope-hope not founded merely on desires and aspirations blit on appreciable facts-that victory will bring us measurably near to an era when war will have become So odious, that the nation which would attempt it, would have to face the majesty and combined strength of the whole civilized world.
I am glad- the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition thought it proper to put his views in this -shape s-o that the people of Canada -might know clearly and distinctly where he stands on this -question of what we should -do for the prosecution of the war-the establishment of peace and the continued unity -and strength of the great Empire to which we belong. I *do not know how it strikes other bon. gentlemen, -but to m-e it is -a s-ad thing to see small, I might almost say contemptible, people in this country trying to -make capital out of the -fact .that the great man who lea-d-s the Opposition happens to be of French ancestry and to speak the French language, trying to give the impression that this must make him disloyal to his King and country trying to " play politics " with this contemptible idea, even at a time when we are in the midst of this great struggle and when every man should bend his thoughts and energies to the one purpose of winning the war. But let me assure my great leader that, so far as Nova Scotia is -concerned and so far as the Maritime Provinces -are concerned, we have known him too long and too well, we have too much faith in him, for -such ideas to have any hold- upon us; that he stands with u-s as our leader our beloved leader, a -leader in whom the -people have always had confidence that he would be loyal and devoted in the performance of his public duties. It would be a strange thing indeed if a man did not -show signs of the nationality to which -he -belonged, I can tell this House that while I profess to be as loyal to my King and -country as a man can possibly be, I-should think les-s of my-self than I do if my hedrt did not respond to the memory of the hills -anid- vales of ol-d Scotland. No -man can rise to his full manhood unless he -has -behind him the ideal of his nationality and of his people and of the principles foT which they. -stand. lit does not make me -les-s a Canadian or les-s a Britisher if I have 'a lingering love and regard -for the dear old hills of Scotland; nor d-oes it make a French Canadian les-s a Britisher or les-s capable of being true to the Crown of Great Britain, and to everything that that -Crown and the -British flag represents, because, forsooth, he happens to s-peak

French, or because his ancestors were born in that great country which stands by our side to-day so loyally and so effectively in support of that which is right and true and in the service of the best interests of civilization and humanity.
I have pointed out where the people I have the honour to represent stand in connection with the war and what we purpose doing in connection with it. Criticism is not always pleasant, but, after all, is it not the duty of men who are sent here as representatives of the people to say what they think should be brought to the notice of the Government if there are defects in the administration of affairs at Ottawa. If things are not going as we think they ought to go, does it not seem reasonable that we should give our opinion in a fair and reasonable manner as to what we think ought to be done? Ancient sacred history tells us that certain men may be regarded as watchmen on the watch-towers of their country. The watchman of a constituency is the man who is sent to this House by the free people of that county to represent it. This particularly refers to members of the Opposition, who sit here as watchmen on the tower; and the pronouncement is: Woe unto the watchman if he does not prepare when danger is approaching. It is therefore our duty to point out to the Government their shortcomings and wherein they could do better. If they take our advice, well and good; if not, their blood be on their own head-the responsibility is entirely theirs.
The results that I speak of as having been brought about by our people in connection with this war have been achieved, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) practically in the teeth of the worst kind of maladministration, whether the Government of to-day and the officers who are particularly appointed by it are responsible or not. This is a country in which we have responsible government, and we hold the heads of departments responsible for these things; it is the only source which we can really get at. We have to look to them for the proper administration of affairs; if they fall short of what we expect them to do, we have to bring it to their notice, and if they do not comply with our fair and reasonable requests, we can only do like Paul of old: we shall appeal to Caesar and to Caesar we shall go. The people of this country will be the Caesar; the people of this country will judge them upon their merits. If, as
I have said, we do not point out these things, the fault will be ours. We do not object to proper expenditures of money, but we must have parliamentary responsibility for these expenditures. I must point out to the parties responsible for the administration of the Militia Department that this has not been the case. We have already pointed out to you, Mr. Speaker, that in the province of Nova Scotia we had some transactions in connection with military matters in which no business ability was shown. We have in this House and in committee dealt with such an important matter as the purchase of horses in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, particularly in Nova Scotia. We have had the spectacle in the province of Nova Scotia of a man having been entrusted with the expenditure of something like $100,000 for the purchase of horses for military purposes, and it was acknowledged in this House by no less a person than the Prime Minister that nobody was responsible for this man's appointment. The Prime Minister, speaking in- this House, said that he should never have been appointed; that he had not the age, experience or ability to perform the services for which he had been appointed, and that as a member of the House he should not have accepted the position. The Prime Minister did not know who appointed him; the exMinister of Militia, who was sitting in the House, did not know who had appointed him. Nobody knew anything about his fitness or qualifications. The question was asked: who gave him the money? If there is a place around Ottawa where a man can get $100,000 without anybody appointing him or giving him authority, I think some of us would like to know where that place is. Here was a man who got $100,000 which he cheeked out in Nova Scotia for such horses as you have heard about so often that it would weary you to hear anything further about them. The responsibility is brought home to the Minister of Militia of that day for the expenditure of this money, whether he wants it or not. The people of Nova Scotia and of all Canada will want to know what sort of Government we have when a man can get $100,000 t# expend in this way without anybody knowing where he got it, how he got it, who gave him the authority, or, as an hon. gentleman suggests, what he did with the money. The elementary principles of business teach us that it would be a simple thing to have



this man bonded for the expenditure of $100,000, and that there should be some proper record of bow he got the $100,000 and of what he did with it. The only record however, we have about it is that there was c nsiderable activity around a glue factory for a few' days somewhere in the province of Quebec and that a certain unfortunate man was read out of the House and, to some extent, out of the Tory party. That is all that the people of Nova Scotia and the people of Canada have for their $100,000. And that, sir, is a very small fraction of the mal-administration in matters of this kind connected with the war. I have simply taken this as an illustration, an incident that shows how this thing was done, and the recklessness and carelessness with which the money of the people was expended for no purpose. We hear of certain enterprises, industrial and otherwise, being conducted, not for their own intrinsic value, and not for what they are really producing, but for the purpose of playing the stock markets with their stocks and bonds. That would appear to be to some extent the scheme of the Government in connection with military matters in this country. You may well say that that is an extraordinary statement to make, that the Government was simply going in for the making of money in connection with military affairs in this country. The right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) read a quotation yesterday which is the basis of the statement which I now make. That is a statement made by the late Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes) in the correspondence between him and the Prime Minister, in which the late minister says that on one occasion he was held up for four long months in carrying on what he had to do in connection with certain contingents, because, forsooth, certain parties wanted to make money out of the business of buying trucks, so that for these four months that contingent was held up. The language of the Minister of Militia is to be found on page 26 of the Hansard of yesterday, and is there quoted from the minister's letter, so that if it is not correctly given there has been ample opportunity of correcting it in this House, as the right hon. Prime Minister spoke after the conclusion of the speech of the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). This is what was said by the exMinister of Militia, as quoted in this House yesterday:-
It is difficult for me to recall where you have actively supported me in the passage of

any Order in Council concerning the upbuilding of the militia when opposed by two Members of the Cabinet usually antagonistic to anything proposed by me. As you are aware, it took up four months in the midst of this great war to fight through the principles of purchasing, for the Second Division, trucks at the lowest wholesale prices instead of allowing large commissions to local agents who would have nothing whatever to do with securing the order.
That, sir, is the charge, that is the indictment. It is an indictment with, perhaps, only one count, but is one on which, if it were placed before the people of this country, with the evidence that supports it, only one verdict could be returned, and that verdict condemnatory of any government that would sit down wrangling and fighting for four long months over a matter of this kind. It would be bad enough to do so for one week. It would be horrifying to see this done for one day. But here, for four long months, the regiments were held up because there were two men in the Cabinet, two men leading some other factions, I suppose, who wanted to filch money out of the treasury of this country and took contemptible means of getting it, by holding up these contracts for trucks. It was nothing that the sons of Canada were being'knocked down like nine pins at the front, that they were killed and torn and slaughtered, with no support to come back up behind them of their own Canadian friends. That was nothing at all. Although we bad the men and the means and the ability to support them, four months had to go by while these men stood with a revolver at the head of this minister, saying: You must give us toll; we stand at the toll gate and you must give us money, otherwise your men cannot get across, we care not what may happen. That is proven to the hilt in the evidence of the minister who wa3 in charge and who wanted to get the business put through. He does not give the names of the members of the Cabinet who did this, but it was evidently done, that is shown beyond peTad-venture. If I wanted to condemn this Government I should not want any stronger indictment than that they, a war government, the war being the principal thing, would delay over this matter for four months, would stand by and see their brethren shot like rabbits in the trenches in France, with no support going to them, all held back for the miserable and contemptible purpose of making a few dollars out of the trucks and wagons that would have to be taken over with this contingent, -
I think I have fulfilled my contract with the leader of the House, and possibly he will

allow me to move the adjournment of the debate.
On motion of Mr. McKenzie, the debate was adjourned.
On motion of Hon. Mr. Rogers, the House adjourned at ten o'clock p.m.
Wednesday, January 24, 1917.
